title: DPO and Preference Optimization
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# DPO and Preference Optimization ##### Four models became two, and the run finished The Mumbai team from Day 14 spent three weeks on PPO. Four models in memory, a reward model that needed its own training run, an adaptive KL controller they tuned by hand, and two runs that diverged for reasons they never fully diagnosed. They switched to DPO. The entire pipeline became: ```python from trl import DPOTrainer, DPOConfig trainer = DPOTrainer(model=policy, ref_model=ref, args=config, train_dataset=preference_data, tokenizer=tokenizer) trainer.train() ``` No reward model. No PPO loop. No generation during training. Two models instead of four. It finished in six hours on the same hardware where PPO had taken three days, and win-rate against the SFT baseline was 68% versus PPO's 71%. Three points of quality for a tenth of the complexity. **For most teams that is not a close call.** Rafailov et al.'s 2023 insight was that the RLHF objective has a **closed-form optimal policy**, and you can therefore skip the reward model entirely and optimise the policy directly on preference pairs. Today is how, and when the alternatives are better. ##### The derivation, briefly Day 14's RLHF objective: $$\max_\pi \; \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi}\big[r(x,y)\big] - \beta \, \mathrm{KL}\big[\pi \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}\big]$$ This has a known optimum: $$\pi^*(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)} \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x) \exp\!\left(\frac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\right)$$ Rearrange for the reward: $$r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x)$$ **The reward is expressible in terms of the policy itself.** Substitute this into the Bradley-Terry preference model and the intractable partition function `Z(x)` cancels, because it depends only on the prompt and appears in both terms of the difference: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\mathbb{E}\left[\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}\right)\right] $$ That is a supervised loss. No sampling, no reward model, no RL. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PPO["RLHF with PPO"] A1["Preference data"] --> B1["Train reward model"] B1 --> C1["PPO loop:
generate → score →
advantage → update"] D1["4 models in memory"] -.-> C1 C1 --> E1["Aligned policy"] end subgraph DPO["DPO"] A2["Preference data"] --> C2["Direct gradient step
on (chosen, rejected)"] D2["2 models in memory"] -.-> C2 C2 --> E2["Aligned policy"] end ``` ##### Implementing DPO ```python import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def get_batch_logps(logits, labels, average=False, ignore_index=-100): """Sum log-probabilities of the label tokens.""" logits = logits[:, :-1, :] labels = labels[:, 1:].clone() mask = labels != ignore_index labels[~mask] = 0 per_token = torch.gather( logits.log_softmax(-1), dim=2, index=labels.unsqueeze(2) ).squeeze(2) if average: return (per_token * mask).sum(-1) / mask.sum(-1).clamp(min=1) return (per_token * mask).sum(-1) def dpo_loss(policy_chosen_logps, policy_rejected_logps, ref_chosen_logps, ref_rejected_logps, beta=0.1, label_smoothing=0.0, loss_type="sigmoid"): """Core DPO loss. All inputs are (batch,) summed log-probs.""" pi_logratios = policy_chosen_logps - policy_rejected_logps ref_logratios = ref_chosen_logps - ref_rejected_logps logits = pi_logratios - ref_logratios # the implicit reward margin if loss_type == "sigmoid": losses = ( -F.logsigmoid(beta * logits) * (1 - label_smoothing) - F.logsigmoid(-beta * logits) * label_smoothing ) elif loss_type == "hinge": losses = torch.relu(1 - beta * logits) elif loss_type == "ipo": # length-robust variant losses = (logits - 1 / (2 * beta)) ** 2 else: raise ValueError(loss_type) chosen_rewards = beta * (policy_chosen_logps - ref_chosen_logps).detach() rejected_rewards = beta * (policy_rejected_logps - ref_rejected_logps).detach() return losses.mean(), { "rewards/chosen": chosen_rewards.mean().item(), "rewards/rejected": rejected_rewards.mean().item(), "rewards/margin": (chosen_rewards - rejected_rewards).mean().item(), "rewards/accuracy": (chosen_rewards > rejected_rewards).float().mean().item(), } ``` **The implicit reward** `β·log(π_θ/π_ref)` is worth understanding. DPO never trains a reward model, but it defines one implicitly, and `rewards/margin` is the diagnostic equivalent of PPO's reward curve. ##### Beta The single most important hyperparameter, playing the role PPO's KL coefficient played. $$\beta \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; \text{stay closer to } \pi_{\text{ref}}$$ | Beta | Behaviour | Use when | |---|---|---| | 0.01 | Aggressive; can degenerate | Rarely | | **0.1** | **Standard default** | Most cases | | 0.3 | Conservative | Small or noisy preference data | | 0.5+ | Barely moves from SFT | Very high-quality SFT already | ```python def diagnose_dpo_run(metrics_history): """Read the reward curves to decide whether beta is right.""" latest = metrics_history[-1] margin = latest["rewards/margin"] chosen = latest["rewards/chosen"] acc = latest["rewards/accuracy"] if chosen < -1.0: return "chosen reward strongly negative → beta too low, policy degenerating" if margin < 0.2: return "margin barely moving → beta too high, or data too noisy" if acc > 0.98 and margin > 8: return "likely overfitting the preference set → fewer epochs" return "healthy" ``` **Watch `rewards/chosen` specifically.** A subtle DPO failure mode: the loss only requires the *margin* to grow, which it can do by pushing the rejected response's likelihood down hard while also lowering the chosen response's likelihood. Both drop, the margin grows, the loss falls — and the model gets worse at everything. If `rewards/chosen` goes strongly negative, raise beta. ##### Training with TRL ```python from trl import DPOTrainer, DPOConfig from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer from peft import LoraConfig import torch model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "./sft-model", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="flash_attention_2", ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("./sft-model") config = DPOConfig( output_dir="./dpo-support", beta=0.1, loss_type="sigmoid", learning_rate=5e-7, # ← VERY low. Note the exponent. lr_scheduler_type="cosine", warmup_ratio=0.1, num_train_epochs=1, # ← usually 1 per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=8, max_length=1024, max_prompt_length=512, bf16=True, gradient_checkpointing=True, eval_strategy="steps", eval_steps=50, logging_steps=10, seed=42, ) # LoRA gives you the reference model for free — disable the adapter peft_config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM") trainer = DPOTrainer( model=model, ref_model=None, # inferred from the base when using PEFT args=config, train_dataset=preference_dataset, # columns: prompt, chosen, rejected eval_dataset=eval_preferences, tokenizer=tokenizer, peft_config=peft_config, ) trainer.train() ``` **Two settings people get wrong:** **Learning rate 5e-7 to 5e-6.** That is 10–100× lower than SFT. DPO's gradients are large because the loss directly manipulates likelihood ratios, and a "normal" fine-tuning learning rate destroys the model within a few hundred steps. **One epoch.** DPO overfits preference data fast. Two epochs is sometimes acceptable on large datasets; three is almost always too many. **`ref_model=None` with PEFT** is a genuine efficiency win — the reference model is the base with the adapter disabled, so you hold one set of weights instead of two. ##### ORPO ORPO (Hong et al., 2024) — Odds Ratio Preference Optimization — removes the reference model entirely by combining SFT and preference learning in a single stage. $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{ORPO}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(y_w) + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{OR}}$$ where the odds ratio term penalises the rejected response relative to the chosen one: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{OR}} = -\log \sigma\!\left(\log \frac{\text{odds}_\theta(y_w|x)}{\text{odds}_\theta(y_l|x)}\right), \qquad \text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}$$ ```python def orpo_loss(policy_chosen_logps, policy_rejected_logps, lambda_or=0.1): """Reference-free: SFT loss on chosen + odds-ratio penalty.""" # log odds = log p - log(1 - p), with p from average token logprob log_odds_chosen = policy_chosen_logps - torch.log1p(-torch.exp(policy_chosen_logps)) log_odds_rejected = policy_rejected_logps - torch.log1p(-torch.exp(policy_rejected_logps)) or_loss = -F.logsigmoid(log_odds_chosen - log_odds_rejected) sft_loss = -policy_chosen_logps # standard NLL on chosen return (sft_loss + lambda_or * or_loss).mean() ``` **ORPO's practical advantage is that it replaces SFT + DPO with one stage.** You go from base model to aligned model in a single training run, holding one model in memory. On a limited GPU budget that is significant. Note that ORPO uses **length-averaged** log probabilities rather than sums, which gives it some inherent length-bias resistance. ##### KTO KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024) — Kahneman-Tversky Optimization — solves a different problem: **it does not need pairs.** DPO and ORPO require `(chosen, rejected)` for the same prompt. Real production feedback is usually a thumbs-up or thumbs-down on a single response, with no counterfactual. ```python def kto_loss(policy_logps, ref_logps, labels, beta=0.1, desirable_weight=1.0, undesirable_weight=1.0, kl_estimate=None): """labels: 1 for desirable, 0 for undesirable. No pairing required.""" logratios = policy_logps - ref_logps kl = kl_estimate if kl_estimate is not None else logratios.mean().clamp(min=0).detach() desirable = labels == 1 losses = torch.zeros_like(logratios) losses[desirable] = desirable_weight * ( 1 - torch.sigmoid(beta * (logratios[desirable] - kl)) ) losses[~desirable] = undesirable_weight * ( 1 - torch.sigmoid(beta * (kl - logratios[~desirable])) ) return losses.mean() ``` The name comes from prospect theory — the loss is asymmetric, reflecting that humans weigh losses more heavily than equivalent gains. `undesirable_weight` above 1.0 makes the model avoid bad outputs more strongly than it seeks good ones. **KTO is the right choice when your feedback is production thumbs up/down**, which is the common case for a deployed product. It also tolerates class imbalance — you rarely get equal numbers of positive and negative ratings. ##### Comparison | | PPO-RLHF | DPO | ORPO | KTO | |---|---|---|---|---| | Reward model | **Required** | No | No | No | | Reference model | Required | Required | **No** | Required | | Models in memory | 4 | 2 | **1** | 2 | | Data format | Pairs | Pairs | Pairs | **Single + label** | | Needs SFT first | Yes | Yes | **No** | Yes | | Stability | Low | High | High | High | | Compute | Very high | Moderate | **Low** | Moderate | | Online improvement | **Yes** | No | No | No | | Typical quality | Highest ceiling | ~95–100% of PPO | ~95% | ~90–95% | **When each wins:** - **DPO** — the default. You have preference pairs and an SFT model. - **ORPO** — limited compute, going from base to aligned in one run. - **KTO** — your feedback is unpaired thumbs up/down from production. - **PPO** — you need online iterative improvement, have the infrastructure, and the last few points matter. Frontier labs still use it. **Other variants worth knowing:** **IPO** replaces the sigmoid with a squared loss and is more robust to overfitting on deterministic preferences; **SimPO** is reference-free with length normalisation; **CPO** merges DPO with an SFT term. ##### Preference data for DPO ```python def build_preference_dataset(records): """DPO expects prompt / chosen / rejected as plain strings.""" return [{ "prompt": r["prompt"], "chosen": r["chosen"], "rejected": r["rejected"], } for r in records] def validate_preference_data(dataset, tokenizer, max_length=1024): """Catch the problems that silently degrade DPO.""" import numpy as np issues, chosen_lens, rejected_lens = [], [], [] for i, ex in enumerate(dataset): c = len(tokenizer(ex["chosen"])["input_ids"]) r = len(tokenizer(ex["rejected"])["input_ids"]) chosen_lens.append(c) rejected_lens.append(r) if ex["chosen"].strip() == ex["rejected"].strip(): issues.append((i, "identical responses")) if c > max_length or r > max_length: issues.append((i, "exceeds max_length — will be truncated")) if not ex["prompt"].strip(): issues.append((i, "empty prompt")) length_bias = np.mean(chosen_lens) / max(np.mean(rejected_lens), 1) return { "n": len(dataset), "issues": issues[:20], "mean_chosen_tokens": int(np.mean(chosen_lens)), "mean_rejected_tokens": int(np.mean(rejected_lens)), "length_ratio": round(float(length_bias), 2), "warning": ("chosen responses are systematically longer — the model will " "learn verbosity" if length_bias > 1.25 else ""), } ``` **The length ratio check is the important one.** If chosen responses average 1.4× the length of rejected ones, DPO will faithfully learn that longer is better — reproducing PPO's length hacking without any RL involved. Either rebalance the data or use IPO/SimPO, which are length-normalised. **On-policy versus off-policy.** DPO works best when the preference data was generated by the model you are tuning, or something close to it. Using pairs generated by GPT-4 to tune a Llama model is off-policy and works less well, because the responses lie outside your model's distribution. If you can, generate candidates from your own SFT model and have those ranked. ##### Evaluation Preference-tuned models need preference-based evaluation, not just loss. ```python from itertools import product def win_rate(model_a, model_b, prompts, judge_fn, tokenizer, n_per_prompt=1): """Pairwise win rate with position randomisation.""" import random wins = {"a": 0, "b": 0, "tie": 0} for prompt in prompts: resp_a = generate(model_a, tokenizer, prompt) resp_b = generate(model_b, tokenizer, prompt) # Randomise order to counter the judge's position bias if random.random() < 0.5: verdict = judge_fn(prompt, resp_a, resp_b) else: verdict = {"a": "b", "b": "a", "tie": "tie"}[ judge_fn(prompt, resp_b, resp_a)] wins[verdict] += 1 total = sum(wins.values()) return {**wins, "win_rate_a": round(wins["a"] / total, 3)} ``` **Position randomisation is mandatory** — LLM judges have a documented preference for whichever response appears first, and forgetting this inflates results by several points. Also track: **length** (has the model become verbose?), **general benchmarks** (Day 11's forgetting check applies), and **refusal rate** (over-alignment makes models refuse benign requests). ##### Common mistakes - **Learning rate set like SFT** (2e-5) instead of 5e-7 — destroys the model in a few hundred steps. - **More than one epoch**, overfitting the preference set. - **Not monitoring `rewards/chosen`**, missing the both-drop degeneration. - **Beta too low**, producing degenerate output. - **Length-imbalanced preference data**, teaching verbosity. - **Off-policy data** from a very different model. - **No position randomisation** in win-rate evaluation. - **Skipping SFT** before DPO — the reference model should be a decent instruction-follower. - **Reference model that is not the SFT checkpoint** you started from. - **Evaluating only on the preference metric**, missing general-capability regression. - **Assuming DPO is strictly better than PPO.** It is simpler and usually close; PPO still wins for online iterative training. ##### Hands-on: DPO against the SFT baseline Your practical task fine-tunes with DPO on a preference dataset and compares against the SFT baseline. Use UltraFeedback or Anthropic HH, and run `validate_preference_data` first — the length-ratio warning will tell you whether to expect verbosity. Then compute win rate with position randomisation. A well-tuned DPO run should reach 60–70% against SFT; if you get 50%, check the learning rate before anything else. The mini project runs DPO and ORPO on the same data and compares simplicity, stability, and quality. The interesting comparison is not just final quality but the operational difference: ORPO starts from the base model and needs no separate SFT stage, so measure end-to-end wall-clock time from base to aligned. Report peak memory for both — ORPO's single-model requirement is its main selling point. The assignment compares DPO, PPO-RLHF, ORPO, and KTO on data needs, stability, and use cases. Build the comparison table from your own measurements where you have them, and be specific about the decision rule: which one you would choose given paired preference data and an existing SFT model, given only production thumbs-up/down, and given a base model and one GPU. That decision framing is what makes it useful rather than encyclopaedic. ##### Key takeaways - **DPO exploits the closed-form optimum of the RLHF objective**, letting you optimise the policy directly on preference pairs with no reward model and no RL loop. - **Learning rate 5e-7 to 5e-6 and one epoch** — DPO's gradients are large and it overfits preference data fast. - **Watch `rewards/chosen`, not just the margin.** The margin can grow while both likelihoods fall, which means the model is getting worse at everything. - **Check the length ratio in your preference data** — systematically longer chosen responses teach verbosity, reproducing PPO's failure without any RL. - **ORPO removes the reference model and the SFT stage; KTO removes the need for pairs** — pick by what your data and compute actually look like, not by what is newest.
